en: Regarding the establishment of the universal *tejastva* (fire-ness) in atoms, [the author] says "of that" (*tasya*) to address this point.
The meaning is that it possesses the nature of fire (*tejastva*). "Just as the nature of water" means:

just as the universal *jalatva* (water-ness) is established in a water atom by virtue of being the delimiting property of the generative cause (*janakatāvacchedaka*) for that which is delimited by the produced nature of water (*janyajalatva*), so too is [the universal *tejastva*] established in a fire atom by virtue of being the delimiting property of the generative cause for that which is delimited by the produced nature of fire (*janyatejastva*).

The meaning is that the existence of the genus *tejastva* (luminosity) is established. This is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*); it should also be understood that the existence of the genus *tejastva* is established because [the cause] is a cause by way of inherence (*samavāya*).
By the phrase "in the rays of the moon, etc.," the rays of gems and so forth are included. In those cases as well...
[This applies] even to the rays of the moon and so forth. Now, one might ask: "Why is there no perception of heat [in that case]?

To this he says: "But rather... [The phrase] "by the touch of the water contained within that" means by the cold touch of the watery portion situated within the rays of the moon. Now, [one might object]:...
Since the hot touch residing in the eye and other [senses] would result in being perceived because it is not overwhelmed by anything else, he says: "And in the eye, etc.
By the phrase "in the rays of emeralds, etc.," gold is included. There might be color...

"White and luminous" is the root [text]. In this context, "white" is a description of its essential nature (*svarūpa*). This is because there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) if "luminosity" alone were taken as the definition. Luminosity (*bhāsvaratva*) is a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*); it resides exclusively in the form of light (*tejas*) and is pervaded by whiteness (*śuklatva*).

One might object: "Since there is no perception of a substance that does not have color as its object, it would follow that Vaiśvānara and other such things could not be perceived by the eye. This is raised in the phrase *tadrūpāgraha*. [The author replies: If Vaiśvānara and others were not visible to the eye, then the qualities residing in them, such as number and so forth, would also not be visible. Thus ends the Dinakarī commentary on verse 2.
"Because it does not reside in every suitable individual"—this is what is indicated by the word "api" (also).
"By means of a form belonging to another" means "by means of an earthy form alone.
He states another opinion with the words "Vaḍhḍhac14;neḥ, however," regarding fire in the form of gold and so forth.
"Because of its existence therein"—the sense is that, for this reason, there is no impossibility [of the definition]. Regarding the phrase "not subsisting in earth":

the term "not subsisting in earth" is included in order to avoid over-extension (ativyāpti) to earth itself, which would occur if one were to take as the [defining] universal (jāti) the form of "earthness" (pṛthivītva), which does indeed subsist in earth—just as the state of having produced smoke (naimittikadravatva) subsists in earth.

The phrase "subsisting in that which possesses adventitious fluidity" (*naimitikadravatvavadvṛtti*) is included to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to water by taking the genus "water-ness," which does not reside in earth, and to water by taking [the genus] "air-ness" (*vāyutva*), which does not reside in earth; and it is included to exclude over-extension to air by taking the property of being either air or fire (*vāyutejonyataratva*).
Thus [it is] "born" (jatīti).
Dinakarī: "From another's touch and so forth."

The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes smell (*gandha*) and so forth, in order to indicate other reasons such as being the manifester of smell. The term "touch" (*sparśa*) is included to avoid the fallacy of unestablishedness (*asiddhi*), since the eye is the manifester of another's color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. In this context...

Some say: the eye is indeed a grasper that does not grasp what is in contact [with it]. If it were to function as an illuminator by reaching its object, then, like the tongue and other senses, it would perceive what is connected to its own physical location (adhiṣṭhāna); but this is not the case, because it perceives what is not connected to the eyeball (golaka). Furthermore, if...
If the eye were to grasp its object by reaching it, then it would not perceive what is subtler than itself, just as one does not perceive what is larger than oneself;
nor indeed does a nail-filer cut what is to be cut by an axe.

Furthermore, there would be no possibility of perceiving the branch and the moon simultaneously, for if perception occurs through reaching via a sequence of motion— *Note: The original text contains corrupted characters (gṛḍhddhac14;ṇīyātarhi, ie2>, etc. which have been interpreted as "grahītuṃ na śakyeta" (would not be able to grasp) and "dinakarī" (the Dinakarī commentary).*

Perception would occur according to the sequence of proximity, rather than simultaneous apprehension; yet one experiences both the branch and the moon simultaneously as soon as the eyes are opened. Thus, in accordance with the principle that the sense organ must reach its object (*prāpyakāritva*), the eye must be something other than the physical eyeball (*golaka*).

Others maintain that because it is impossible for the eyeball to reach the moon and other distant objects, the eye must function without reaching its object (*aprāpyakāritva*); and since the eyeball itself is the eye, it cannot be composed of light (*taijasa*). This is incorrect, because the eye, like the light of a lamp, can perceive objects not connected to its physical substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Because reaching [the object] is possible, and because the perception of something larger [than the eye] is established— since the eye, though a small globe, issues forth as a large organ with a broad tip, just like the light of a lamp—
and because there is a deviation from such a rule in the case of the sense of touch, which perceives objects larger than itself.
And because there is a lack of evidence;
furthermore, the apprehension of [the two] as being simultaneous is unproven, for that is merely a subjective conviction.

This is because the attainment [of the sun] occurs through its proximity in time. For the excellence of the velocity of light is inconceivable due to the extreme subtlety of its brilliance, such that while the Lord garlanded with rays has not yet even reached the peak of the eastern mountain, there arises the conviction within the interiors of houses that "there is light."
Regarding the worlds,

as the Śālikācāryas have said: "By means of the eye initiated by both the external light and [the internal organ], and being in contact with the object, there is the simultaneous apprehension of that much of the object."

[Objection: It is indeed possible for the moon and its branch to be perceived at the same time. [Reply: That is not so; because the eye, having been produced by the external light and the eye itself, exists even in its posterior part, it would follow that objects situated behind it could be perceived.
Furthermore, there is no evidence for the production of the eye by the external lights located in the region behind it.

Even regarding the external light situated at the foremost point [of the eye], there is no evidence for its production [therein]; for it has just been stated that the production of visual perception is possible even without admitting such [external light]. To state [the conclusion] with parsimony, he says: "Alternatively. As for what the evidence is for [gold] being composed of light (*taijasa*): gold is earthy (*pārthiva*).

Since there exists the inference—"because it possesses occasional liquidity"—which establishes its being earthen, [the opponent] replies: "No. Regarding "gold": there is no sublation (*bādha*) here even if gold, which consists of a substance possessing yellow color, is taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), because luminous gold is not established prior to the inference.

It should not be argued that there is a lack of establishment of the subject (*pakṣāprasiddhi*), because even in the case of a yellow substance mentioned in the Dharmaśāstra, the term "gold" (*suvarṇa*) is employed, and thus it too is denotable by the word "gold. Consequently, if being denotable by the word "gold" were taken as the delimiting property of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*), the defect of sublation (*bādha*) would remain as it was. [This is so] because, upon contact with intense fire...
Since the locus of liquidity that is not being cut off is itself the delimiting condition (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*) [of the subject],
and since the intended goal is the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) by means of that very delimiting condition,
there is no fault arising from the identity between the delimiting condition of the subject and the reason (*hetu*), even though they are co-located (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Because proving what is already established is not a fault. Regarding the phrase "provided there is no obstacle":
the words "provided there is no obstacle" are included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of ghee and the like situated in water.
The word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) is included to exclude deviation in the case of ghee and the like, which possess fluidity that is not destroyed by conjunction with fire.

The phrase ends with "satīti" (provided that...). There is no deviation [in the logical reason], because such fluidity does not exist at the same time as an absolute conjunction with fire that is co-located with it.

The phrase "because its fluidity is not interrupted" means "because it possesses a substratum whose fluidity is not interrupted," and not "because it is not a substratum of interrupted fluidity," for [otherwise] there would be a deviation in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and so forth.
"Because it is destructible by contact with fire"—this is merely an illustration. [From the *Dinakarī*: "The first offspring of Fire..."
This is because the scriptural passage beginning with "hiraṇyam" (gold) serves as a supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) due to its otherwise inexplicability (*anyathānupapatti*).

By this [argument], in order to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the destruction of fluidity (*dravatva*) caused by the destruction of its substratum, [the definition] specifies "in fluidity..."
Having postulated a specific universal (*jāti-viśeṣa*) excluded from the fluidity that is destroyed by the destruction of its substrate,

one must accept that the conjunction with fire (*agni-saṃyoga*) is the cause for the destruction of a fluidity belonging to a different class (*vijātīya*). And that particularity (*vaijātya*) is also excluded from the fluidity of gold (*suvarṇa*).
The argument that favorable reasoning has been shown— namely, that even if gold were earth,
its liquidity would not be subject to destruction by contact with fire because it is not encompassed by the delimitors of destructibility caused by such contact,
and thus the undesirable consequence of its destruction would be impossible even when intense contact with fire exists— is also refuted.

*Kṣoda* means powder. Regarding that [gold], which is the substratum of its yellow color and heaviness, the author presents the view of those who establish its luminous nature (*taijasatva*) by another method, beginning with the words "others, however" (*apare tu*). *Tat-pratibandhaka* means the obstacle to the transformation of color. [This applies] even to the case of fire-contact in the case of luminous gold.

It is stated [in the definition] that "it arises from contact with fire" (*satvāt*). The term "of a different kind" (*vijātīya*) is included in the probandum (*sādhya*) for the purpose of establishing the intended subject.

In the reason (*hetu*), the qualification "being existent" (*satyantam*) is added to prevent the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a jar (*ghaṭa*), which lacks contact with fire and does not possess a form of a different kind from its previous form. Here, "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*) should be supplied to the reason; by that—

There is no deviation [of the reason] in the case of a water-atom (*jalaparamāṇu*). To exclude the case of a jar that has been somehow conjoined with fire, the term "ultimate" (*atyanta*) is included. Nor is the reason unestablished (*aprayojaka*), because the conjunction of earth with fire produces a color of a different genus from the previous color only when there is a connection with a contrary liquid substance.

[This is] the state of being. Nor should it be said that the obstructing factor is something other than a liquid substance, for that would entail the postulation of an unobserved entity (*adṛṣṭa*). [Regarding the phrase] "and of that":
"of that" means of the liquid substance. [The phrase] "distinct from earth and water" means distinct from earth... [and so forth].

The sense is that because there is an absence of dissimilarity (vijātīyatva) in the substance which is the locus of the yellowness under consideration, water cannot exist there. "Due to the non-necessity of being fire" means that there is an absence of color (rūpa) in air and so forth. Nor does it follow that there would be the apprehension of a substance as the locus of the color yellow in darkness.
It should be stated that [the reason] is "because of the existence of the conjunction of gold’s color with light";

for it is precisely the conjunction of manifest and unobscured color with light that is the cause of the perception of a substance, whereas the color of gold is indeed obscured at that time. Nor is this so because, at that time, even the yellow color is not perceived.
The non-perception [of gold] is caused by the perception of its homogeneous [substratum], and not because the form of the gold is overwhelmed;
nor should it be said that its form is overwhelmed, for "overwhelming" (abhibhava) means precisely the connection with a homogeneous [object] due to its lightness. And even so, in the dark...

It should not be argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of the direct perception of gold, because the conjunction with light is a cause only for the perception of substances other than fire; for that [conjunction] is a cause only for the perception of substances other than that fire which is distinct from gold. However, the moderns [hold as follows]:

Gold is indeed earth; for since the cognition "melted gold flows" arises through direct contact, it cannot be an error, as the cognition "it flows more and more" shows that even the fluidity [of gold] is completely destroyed. Thus, [gold] possesses the nature of earth.

They say that because [gold] is the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of yellow color, and because gold is an antagonist (*virodhin*) to the destruction of color by virtue of its identity (*tādātmya*) with it, there is no destruction of the yellow color. Thus ends the section on light (*tejo-grantha*). Now, in order to demonstrate the proof (*pramāṇa*) for air (*vāyu*):

Regarding the statement, "In the root [text], the touch of air is held to be non-produced-by-heat and neither-hot-nor-cold," he explains the exclusion [of other qualities] by the terms "non-produced-by-heat" and so forth, respectively: "the touch is neither-hot-nor-cold.
It was stated that it is "not produced by heat"; for although the possession of a touch that is neither-hot-nor-cold and not produced by heat [is a characteristic of air],...

Although [the definition] is over-extended to cloth and the like, its meaning should nevertheless be understood as either: "possessing a genus that is directly pervaded by substancehood (dravyatva) and resides only in that which possesses a touch that is neither produced by heating (apākaja) nor hot-cold (anuṣṇāśīta)," or "possessing a genus that is directly pervaded by substancehood and resides in that which possesses a touch that is neither hot-cold nor produced by heating (pākaja). By this, [it is meant] by the statement that the touch is neither hot nor cold, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the delimiting factor of its production": thus, the universal *vāyutva* (air-ness) is established as the delimiting factor of the production of a specific kind of touch. This is also an illustration: [it may also be established] as the delimiting factor of the efficient causality of a particular sound, or of that which is delimited by the property of being produced by a drum (*bherī*).

It should also be understood that this establishes the existence of the universal *vāyutva* (the property of being air). Regarding the phrase "having touch and so forth as its mark" (*sparśādiliṅgaka*) in the root text:

it means that which has touch and the like as its inferential marks (*liṅga*). Regarding the term "gravity" (*ghṛti*) in the *Muktāvalī*: gravity is the non-falling of a heavy substance. Regarding the phrase "by a heterogeneous touch" (*vijātīyasparśena*): [it refers to a touch distinct from those of earth, water, and fire].

The group of four words ending in the third case (instrumental) is connected with the term "anumānāt" (from inference). As for the method of inference: that touch which does not inhere in a substance possessing color must be supported by something, because it is a touch, like the touch inherent in earth; [this being so] regarding the touch of earth and the other elements...
The qualification "inhering in a substance possessing color" is added to avoid the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
Thus, in the absence of an impact from a substance possessing color, this series of sounds occurring in leaves and the like— [is explained as follows].
The *Dinakarī*: [Sound] is produced by the conjunction of a substance possessing touch and velocity,
because it is a series of sounds residing in a substance whose parts are not being divided.

It is like the continuous series of sounds produced by a drum struck by a staff. The qualification of the subject (*pakṣaviśeṣaṇa*) beginning with "not being" (*asati*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*) in the case of sound produced by the impact of earth and other elements. The term "not being divided" (*avibhajyamāna*) in the reason (*hetu*) is for the purpose of avoiding the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of sound produced by disjunction (*vibhāga*). This applies likewise to the ether (*nabhas*).
The suspension of grass, cotton, clouds, celestial chariots (*vimāna*), and so forth,
is caused by conjunction with a substance possessing touch and velocity, because it is the suspension of a substance not presided over by beings such as ourselves,

like the suspension of a boat [in water]. The phrase "in the sky" (*nabhasi*) is included to exclude the possibility of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanavāraṇa*) in the case of grass and other objects situated in water and the like.

The term "of us and others" (*asmadādīnām*) is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as the upward motion (*ūrdhvagati*) caused by the conjunction of the self with one who exerts effort.
Similarly, the motion in a blade of grass occurs without the impact of a material substance possessing color;
it is produced by the impact of a substance possessing touch and velocity, because it is a type of motion belonging to a different class (*vijātīyakarman*).

"Like the action of *kāśa* grass and other plants struck by the swelling of a river. "It will be explained later" means at the occasion of the investigation into the self (*ātman*). [End of Dinakarī].
"At the root, eternality and so forth are stated as before" means that it is like water, as previously described.
By the phrase "eternality and so forth," non-eternality is included. The meaning is that what was stated should be understood.
He clarifies this very point in the *Muktāvalī*: "Air is of two kinds. Among those...

"In the middle" means "born not from a womb" (ayonija), that is to say, born without a womb. Regarding the phrase "of the Piśācas and so forth," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "it is well known in the world of the Maruts. Now, one might object:
since Vāyu lacks the vocal apparatus such as the palate and so on, and lacks hands, feet, and the like...
To the question, "In the absence of movement, maintenance, and so forth, how can there be the status of being a locus for experience? he says:

"But [the case is] supreme," etc. Since the refutation regarding the watery and fiery bodies is identical, he speaks generally with the intention of achieving brevity of the treatise (*prakaraṇalāghava*).
He states the resolution: "It consists of the watery, fiery, and airy [elements]. But how, then, is there the designation of it as "watery" and so forth?

To this he says: "Of water and the others. Here, "in the sense organ of touch" refers to that specific quality, such as its substratum and so on. [The commentary] Dinakarī states: "Pervading the body. And not...
It should not be said that [the sense of touch] is impossible in the case of nails, body hair, head hair, and so forth, because they do not serve as the substratum for the sense of touch;
for these lack the status of being a "body" (*śarīra*) since they are merely substances joined [to it].
As for the expression "the sense of touch located in the root," its meaning is "the sense organ situated in the skin. By this—

The innate covering of the body is called the skin (*tvak*); and since it is composed of earth (*pārthiva*) and is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣasiddha*), the [objection] that it is neither a sense organ nor composed of air (*vāyavīya*) is refuted.
He states the definition of the tactile organ (*tvagindriya*) as follows: "touch," etc.
The term "sense organ" (*indriya*) is used to exclude over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to time and so forth, which produce only effects.
The phrase "perceiver of touch" (*sparśagrāhaka*) is used to exclude over-extension to the eyes and other [senses].
"The skin" (*tvak*) means the tactile sense organ (*tvagindriya*). "And that" (*tac ca*) means "and the tactile sense organ. This refers to the subject (*pakṣa*).

The phrase "among color and the rest" (*rūpādiṣu madhye*) is used to avoid the charge of being unestablished (*asiddhi*) because [the quality] manifests touch. The word "only" (*eva*) is used to avoid deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to the mind (*manas*). It should also be understood that the phrase "while being a substance" (*dravyatve sati*) is included to avoid deviation with respect to the contact of the tactile organ (*tvagindriya-sannikarṣa*). [This refers to] water clinging to the body.

Sweat. || 43 || [This is] in the *Ākara*, the *Praśastapādabhāṣya*, and other such works. As for the statement that "the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is indeed one," how then is there the conventional usage of terms such as "downward breath" (*apāna*) and so forth? To this he says: "by virtue of its locations. "The *prāṇa* is in the heart, the *apāna* in the anus, the *samāna* is situated in the navel, the *udāna* resides in the region of the throat, and the *vyāna*..."

The phrase "pervading the entire body" means [the distinction] due to the difference in location. And "due to the difference in function": because it exits and enters through the mouth and nose, it is *prāṇa*;
because it leads waste products downward, it is *apāna*; and because it maintains the digestive fire for the sake of cooking food, it is *samāna*.

It is called *samāna* because it leads [the breath] evenly (*samunnayanāt*); it is called *udāna* because it leads [it] upwards (*udūrdhvaṃ nayanāt*); and it is called *vyāna* because it extends [it] through the openings of the channels (*nāḍīmukheṣu vitananāt*). Thus, it receives five designations due to the difference in its functions; the point is that there is no difference in the entity designated by the fact that its designations differ. This concludes the section on Air (*vāyu*). [From] Dinakarī: "Ākāśa... etc.

It will be stated later that "temporality" (kālatva) and "spatiality" (diktva) are not universals (jāti); for the sake of brevity, this has been mentioned here incidentally. "Not a universal"—the remainder of the argument is that this is because they lack inherence in multiple individuals (anekasamavetatvābhāvāt).
Thus, the fact of having only a single individual instance is the reason for the absence of being a universal. (Dinakari)

The objection regarding "residing in different substrata" (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) has been answered. As for the phrase "but what [is the case]": here, "being a substratum" is intended in the sense of *samavāya* (inherence);
therefore, there is no flaw even if time is the substratum of sound by virtue of being the substratum of the entire universe.
Suspecting that the word "Vaiśeṣika" in the root text might be redundant, he says: "as for the term 'Vaiśeṣika'..."

And thus, the root text "and sound" (*itthaṃ ca śabdaḥ*) should be understood as being restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*). By this statement regarding its being a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), the proof (*pramāṇa*) is established, beginning with the words "in ether" (*ākāśa*) and so forth. And that [proof] is: sound resides in a substance other than the eight substances such as earth, because while it does not reside in those eight substances, [it is nonetheless a quality].
It should be understood that [the reason] is of the form "because of being dependent on a substance. It has been shown—that is, indicated.

Here, in order to avoid the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the essence (*svarūpāsiddhi*) in this inference, he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*). The term "impossible" (*ayogya*) is used to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a jar and so forth. To exclude deviation in the case of the self (*ātman*), [the term "impossible" is used].

"Perceptible by the external sense organs" is stated to exclude [properties] such as *rasatva* (tasteness). "Possessing a genus" (*jātimat*) is included to avoid the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the reason (*svarūpāsiddhi*) in the subsequent inference that establishes its inherence in a substance. "Because it is a quality" (*guṇatvāt*).
By this inference, the unestablished nature of the qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddhi*) in the reason of the aforementioned *pariśeṣa* (method of elimination) inference has been refuted.
To remove the unestablished nature of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*), he says: "Sound is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of that which possesses touch.
The meaning is: [sound] is not a specific quality of the four substances possessing touch, such as earth and the rest. This is the sense.

"Because it is perceptible and not preceded by qualities in its cause. This means: because it is perceptible while being non-preceded by qualities in its cause. To establish the existence of the reason, [the author says] "produced by baking" (*pākaja*). [He says] "of the water-atom" (*jalaparamāṇu*), because some of the non-eternal qualities of earth, such as color and so forth, have conjunction with fire as their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*).
In some cases, there is indifference here because [the property] is preceded by the qualities of its cause. [The phrase] "not space or time" follows from the word "sound.

[The term] "external sense organ" means a sense organ other than the mind; the meaning is that it is perceptible due to its suitability [for perception]. By this, [it is established that sound is not a quality of space or time] because it is perceived by a sense organ that does not grasp the qualities of the self.

The state of being an external sense organ is also over-extended to the mind (*manas*), since by that [mind] too there is the apprehension of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; thus, it is completely rejected. And in this manner, when the non-dependence on the six substances such as earth is established, [the conclusion] is established. The meaning is that it is established by the aforementioned *pariśeṣa* (residual) inference.

[Objection: "But all this would be possible only if there were some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for sound being a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*); we do not see any such proof in that regard. [Reply: No; for sound is a specific quality, because it is perceptible by a sense organ through ordinary contact (*laukikapratyāsatti*), while [at the same time] it is not perceptible by a sense organ through ordinary contact [with its own substratum].
